report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is false. No scientific evidence supports a link between approved apple waxes and cancer.

**Evidence:**

The waxes used on apples—primarily carnauba wax, beeswax, and shellac—are natural substances approved by the FDA for food use. Apples naturally produce their own waxy coating to protect against moisture loss and disease; commercial wax is applied after harvest simply to replace what gets scrubbed off during washing (Science Insights, 2026; McGill University).

Snopes explicitly fact-checked the viral rumor and concluded that the wax used on apples is safe to eat and that the cancer claim is unfounded (Snopes, 2016). Multiple health and science sources confirm the same: the current scientific consensus is that FDA-approved wax coatings on apples are not considered carcinogenic, and no human studies support the claim (Fertile Hope, 2025; Wellnd, 2025). Health Digest (2024) specifically noted that TikTok posts claiming paraffin wax on apples causes cancer are misleading, as food-grade paraffin wax is considered edible and safe.

The waxes serve a beneficial purpose—reducing water loss, slowing deterioration, and extending shelf life. Without edible coatings, over a third of apple production would be wasted before reaching retailers (ScienceDirect, 2023).
